newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaiti men vote for new parliament.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaiti men vote for new parliament.

text.p: Security concerns top the list of priorities when Kuwait votes on Monday in its second election since the 1991 Gulf War ended Iraq's seven-month occupation of the oil-rich state.
The new 50-member chamber is expected to press for further defence measures to deter Iraq, while also seeking stronger powers to monitor state spending and tackle alleged corruption.

Analysts forecast that more than 70 percent of the 107,000-strong all-male electorate would vote. Polls open at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) for 12 hours. About 230 candidates, including 41 members of the outgoing parliament, are standing.
Leading Moslem Shi'ite candidate Adnan Abdul-Samad told an election rally that voting was more important than choosing a husband for your daughter.
"Those who sell their votes are selling a right to have a voice for four years," he said in reference to alleged vote-buying.

A Western diplomat earlier told Reuters that, despite repeated allegations of vote-buying by pro-government and other candidates, none of the leading politicians were questioning the fairness of the process or calling for international monitoring.

The state has repeatedly said its role in the election was purely administrative. Leading members of the ruling al-Sabah family, eager to maintain an image of neutrality, were not expected to vote, officials said.
Heated election competitions have triggered some Kuwaiti fears of sectarian differences emerging between the Moslem Sunni majority and the Shi'ites who make up just over a quarter of the population..

Shi'ite candidate Abdul-Mohsen Jamal, a former member of parliament, told Reuters sectarian primaries "shred national unity and create sensitivities between the people of the one nation. But I think all of this will be erased in the future."
The election is traditionally followed by the government's resignation and the formation of a new one by Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah, Kuwait's crown prince and prime minister.

The outgoing parliament, the only elected house in the six Gulf Arab states, was no rubber stamp. It opened probes into alleged official corruption and claims of poor government management before Iraq's 1990 invasion and occupation of Kuwait.
Speaker Ahmad al-Saadoun said in his closing address that parliament "defended public funds and held accountable those who allowed themselves to violate its sanctuary."
He had earlier criticised the state for not moving fast enough to rebuild the military five years after the war.
The parliament's last act was to approve a $14 billion state budget for 1996/97 with a $4 billion deficit. The government says it plans to balance the budget by 2000.
